articles.title: Iran will not trade its nuclear insurance policy for worthless American promises
articles.summary:
Iran will not trade its nuclear insurance policy for worthless American promises

Submitted by Ali Naghieh on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 15:45
A durable agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz must make concessions progressively harder to reverse on both sides
Iranian missiles are seen on display near a portrait of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, at Baharestan Square in Tehran on 28 September 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off

US President Donald Trump last month rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations, while hinting that talks might continue. But the fundamental barrier to a lasting agreement is Washington’s habit of rewriting the rules after the ink dries. 

Consider the last diplomatic opening. The June memorandum between the US and Iran promised to release frozen funds for recipients chosen by Iran’s central bank. 

Five days later, US Vice President JD Vance outlined a different arrangement: Washington and Qatar would approve the process, while the money would be restricted to purchases of American soy, corn and wheat. Washington was writing a shopping list with Iran’s money. 

That bait-and-switch highlighted a fatal flaw in American diplomacy. Washington expects Iran to trade lasting nuclear dismantlement for benefits the US can withdraw overnight. 

The more nuclear capacity Tehran surrenders, the more it depends on its adversary’s whims to deliver the rewards. Without enforceable, symmetrical remedies for American non-compliance, Washington’s preferred bargain leaves Iran easier to coerce precisely because it complied.

The US justified withdrawing oil and banking relief by citing Iranian attacks on shipping. But treating those clashes as the beginning of the story ignores the diplomatic sabotage that preceded them. 

Under the June interim agreement, Washington agreed to lift its naval blockade and grant oil waivers in exchange for a halt in hostilities and Iranian cooperation to restore Hormuz transit, pending Iranian-Omani talks over maritime administration. Tehran agreed to facilitate passage, not to surrender maritime oversight. 

Yet just one day later, a US-backed maritime centre recommended a southern route through Omani waters to bypass northern lanes associated with Iranian control. Washington was thus demanding Iranian cooperation, while simultaneously plotting a route to reduce Tehran’s leverage over Hormuz. 

When Iranian forces opened fire on 25 June on a vessel using the uncoordinated bypass route, the deal’s cooperative premise had already dissolved into a raw contest for control. 

Hollow promises

The promised financial relief proved equally hollow. By late June, Qatar confirmed that the mechanism for releasing Iran’s frozen funds remained unresolved, while Washington’s proposed arrangement restricted the money to purchases of American agricultural goods - tying Iran’s access to its own sovereign assets to Washington’s domestic priorities. 

When further clashes erupted in July, the US Department of the Treasury revoked oil authorisations just 16 days after issuing them. It took no election or new administration; the same White House that granted relief quickly snatched it back. 

Washington treats its unilateral discretion to reverse commitments as strategic leverage. For Tehran, that discretion is precisely what makes American commitments unreliable.

Washington has spent years dictating what Iran must surrender; the next deal must also ask what the US will put beyond its own discretion

Iran has already experienced the consequences of substantial nuclear concessions. Under the 2015 nuclear agreement, it reduced its enriched-uranium stockpile, dismantled centrifuges, and rendered the Arak reactor vessel unusable. Trump withdrew from the deal in May 2018, while the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed Iran’s full compliance; Tehran waited more than a year before scaling back its commitments. 

Inspectors could verify the surrendered uranium and dismantled centrifuges, but they could not verify whether Washington would honour its commitments. Rebuilding a disabled reactor takes years, while reimposing US sanctions takes a single “stroke of a pen”. 

Regional war has transformed this imbalance into a security dilemma. For Tehran, nuclear latency - the ability to move quickly towards a weapon without actually possessing one - is increasingly viewed not simply as bargaining leverage, but as strategic insurance against catastrophic and existential escalation. 

Nuclear latency has not deterred conventional strikes. But the prospect of a rapid nuclear breakout forces adversaries to calibrate their campaigns: pushing for state collapse leaves a cornered Iran with no choice but to finally build the bomb.

Fatal paradox

Herein lies the fatal paradox of Washington’s strategy. The war might have reduced Iran’s nuclear capacity, but it also increased the value Tehran attaches to retaining a nuclear hedge. American policymakers treat military escalation as leverage to compel nuclear surrender, blind to the fact that the pressure itself makes surrender suicidal.

Demanding that Tehran dismantle its hedge, without altering the threats that make it valuable, risks turning military gains into diplomatic failure. Washington can destroy facilities; it cannot expect the same campaign to make nuclear restraint more acceptable. 

If compliance leaves Tehran more exposed to the next bombing campaign, Washington is not preventing a bomb, but rather manufacturing the strategic necessity for it.

Any new agreement must include restoring full IAEA access. Negotiators cannot freeze a stockpile that inspectors cannot monitor. But demanding transparency requires acknowledging Tehran’s intelligible pessimism: having watched the agency fail to unequivocally condemn attacks on its nuclear facilities, Tehran views intrusive inspections not as a routine baseline, but as a major security concession. 

Once stockpiles are verified and immobilised, deeper reductions, such as diluting 60 percent material, must strictly follow demonstrated American performance: actual oil sales, accessible sovereign assets, and an enduring ceasefire.

This requires reciprocal irreversibility: reversible steps, such as immobilising nuclear material, should initially be exchanged for reversible measures, such as sanctions waivers. Progressively harder-to-reverse concessions, such as downblending, should be matched by progressively harder-to-revoke economic and security commitments from Washington. 

That means moving up a durability ladder, from flimsy presidential waivers towards normalised banking access, sovereign funds secured in independent international escrow, congressional repeal of statutory sanctions, and deeper long-term commercial integration with the global economy. Permanent Iranian nuclear concessions cannot be purchased with temporary presidential promises. 

Another countdown

Economic relief alone cannot resolve a security crisis. Washington cannot demand that Iran surrender its nuclear hedge, while simultaneously underwriting the threat that gives that hedge much of its value. 

The US must formally pledge not to launch unprovoked strikes against a compliant Iran, while explicitly withholding intelligence, aerial refuelling, base access and munitions that could be used in an Israeli attack. Should Israel strike a compliant Iran anyway, the agreement must mandate an automatic suspension of specified US offensive military aid. 

Can Iran war deadlock be broken at the US ballot box?
Read More »

To enforce boundaries, dispute resolution must be independent and insulated from unilateral political vetoes. If Washington withholds earned relief, or if the US or Israel strike a compliant Iran, an independent panel established at signing should clear Tehran to halt nuclear reductions and suspend deal-specific restrictions, without losing economic relief already secured. 

Iran would remain bound by the baseline safeguards of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and verified Iranian violations would trigger predetermined consequences, including a rapid sanctions snapback. 

Beyond the agreement itself, a durable settlement requires a transformed regional security architecture. Iran’s neighbours have legitimate concerns over maritime disruption and cross-border escalation. The nuclear pact should therefore run alongside a regional security process - one involving Iran, Iraq, and the six Gulf Cooperation Council states - that explores cooperative frameworks like a regional fuel-cycle consortium. 

This would allow Iran to retain domestic enrichment under shared regional ownership and oversight, thus reducing mutual threats, rather than substituting American hegemony for Iranian dominance.

The objective is not simply to delay an Iranian bomb, but to reduce the strategic incentive to build one in the first place. That requires a regional security environment in which remaining without a nuclear deterrent is strategically sustainable for Tehran. 

No agreement can erase Iran’s nuclear knowledge, but a durable settlement can reduce the strategic value of turning that knowledge into a weapon. Washington has spent years dictating what Iran must surrender; the next deal must also ask what the US will put beyond its own discretion. If the answer is nothing, another signature will simply buy another countdown.

articles.title: Israel turns back Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight over Indonesian pilot's nationality
articles.summary:
Israel turns back Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight over Indonesian pilot's nationality

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 13:05
Israel has barred pilots from 31 nationalities from landing in the country amid new restrictions
People board an Ethiopian Airlines plane at the Bole International Airport, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 17 March 2020 (Eduardo Soteras/AFP)
Off

An Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight bound for Israel was forced to return to Addis Ababa after Israeli authorities refused it permission to land because one of its pilots was Indonesian.

Israel's Channel 13 News reported on Monday that the plane was travelling from Addis Ababa to Tel Aviv when Israeli authorities discovered mid-flight that one of its pilots was an Indonesian citizen.

The plane was instructed to return to Ethiopia, where the Indonesian pilot was replaced by a pilot from a country whose nationals are permitted to fly to Israel, the Israeli news outlet Ynet reported.

The cargo flight subsequently continued to Tel Aviv and landed.

TAL Aviation, which represents Ethiopian Airlines in Israel, told the Israeli news site Ynet that the incident would not affect "passenger flights to Tel Aviv or from it to Addis Ababa".

State-owned Ethiopian Airlines has continued operating flights to Israel despite Israel's genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, and attacks on Lebanon and Iran.

The airline recently announced plans to operate 26 flights a week between Addis Ababa and Tel Aviv.

Israelis to avoid Arab airlines, poll shows

Monday's incident comes less than two weeks after an Omani national serving as a co-pilot on a Flydubai flight bound for Ben Gurion Airport allegedly attempted to hijack the aircraft and crash it at Israel's main international airport.

According to reports, the pilot was apprehended by several Israeli passengers after the plane plunged 16,000 feet in 30 seconds following an altercation between him and the other pilot. The aircraft subsequently landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

On Friday, UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said the Omani pilot had planned a suicide attack on Ben Gurion Airport.

Air France enforces Israeli ban affecting pilots from Muslim countries
Read More »

Shamsi said security procedures had "revealed [no] indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," according to Reuters.

Following the incident, Israel said it was barring pilots from countries it considers hostile or with which it has no diplomatic relations from landing in the country or crossing its airspace.

Israeli authorities published a list of 31 countries that would be affected, and also said the restrictions would apply to dual nationals.

The Transport Ministry has faced accusations of neglecting its responsibility to carry out proper security checks on flights.

The tighter restrictions have also heightened public concern over the nationalities of crew members operating flights to Israel.

More than 40 percent of Israelis said they preferred to fly with Israeli airlines or planned to avoid Arab and Muslim airlines, according to a poll published after the Flydubai incident by Israeli news outlet Mako.

articles.title: British man in Israeli army posed in front of burning Gaza school, new film reveals
articles.summary:
British man in Israeli army posed in front of burning Gaza school, new film reveals

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 15:35
Jonathan Burman went to school in Manchester before joining Israeli army and serving in Gaza, Declassified UK finds
Jonathan Burman in front of the Madrasa al-Farabi in Gaza (Obtained by Declassified UK)
Off

A British man posed in front of a burning school in Gaza while serving with the Israeli army, an investigation by Declassified UK has revealed. 

A film published by Declassified on Tuesday on YouTube entitled "We Exposed a British-Israeli Who Fought in Gaza" features a photograph of a British citizen it names as Jonathan Burman standing as a soldier in the Israeli military in front of the school in Gaza. 

The film documents Declassified's investigation as the news organisation uncovered the details behind the photo, which it said Burman had originally posted on his private Instagram account. 

Airwars, a transparency watchdog, traced the school to the Bani Suheila town east of Khan Younis in Gaza.

The school was called Madrasa al-Farabi. On 12 December 2023, just over two months into the Gaza genocide, it was reported that Israeli soldiers attacked it. 

In response to Declassified's request for comment, the Israeli military sent a statement from December 2023 saying it had eliminated a terrorist cell in a school.

But Airwars found this was a different school two kilometres away from the one in the photo - not the one Burman posed in front of. 

Burman, according to Declassified, attended Manchester Grammar School before going on a gap year in Israel. He later joined the Israeli army.

The Israeli military confirmed to Declassified that Burman served in the 55th Brigade, an elite reserve unit of paratroopers.

According to Declassified, Burman posted a photo on his Instagram account which appeared to show him in Gaza's Khan Younis with heavy destruction visible behind him, as well as photos of himself serving in Lebanon and sitting in military overalls with other soldiers. 

Warrants 'further investigation'

The film says Burman likely served in the brigade's 66th Battalion. It features an interview with Yuval Green, a man who had served in that battalion as a medic.

"Some of the people are really driven by crazy insane religious ideas," Green said. "This [fighting in Gaza] was just an opportunity for them to kill as many Gazans as they can and kick them out and get their lands."

The film also cites research by the Hind Rajab Foundation which identified a company which it believed Burman had "likely" served with. That company was involved in "close combat fighting and blowing up many residential buildings" in Khan Younis, and "laid waste to vast swathes" of the area, according to the foundation's findings.

Chris Sidoti, a member of the United Nations Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, also appears in the Declassified film.

He said Declassified's metholodgy "is exactly the methodology we use in" our investigations. Sido said "you are not saying that this person is guilty of war crimes", but that "the evidence is sufficient" to warrant "further investigation".

Sidoti said that the London Metropolitan Police's war crimes unit should investigate Burman.

Burman himself did not respond to requests for comment, according to Declassified.

Around 2,000 British-Israeli dual nationals are believed to have served in the Israeli military during Israel's war on Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry found was a genocide last year.

Israeli forces have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the Hamas attack on 7 October 2023 which killed 1,200 people, with a further 170,000 wounded. Thousands more in Gaza remain missing and are presumed dead beneath the rubble.

In April, London's Metropolitan Police announced it would not investigate 10 British nationals accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity while fighting with the Israeli military in Gaza.

This came after the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR) and the Public Interest Law Centre (PILC) filed a 240-page dossier to the Met's War Crimes Team in April last year.

The Met said there was no realistic prospect of conviction and that an effective investigation could not be conducted.

articles.title: Azerbaijan accuses Turkey of stoking tensions over headscarf ban
articles.summary:
Azerbaijan accuses Turkey of stoking tensions over headscarf ban

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 12:49
The ruling party in Baku tells Ankara to respect its sovereignty and rejects criticism of its headscarf restrictions and close ties with Israel
Turkish fans gather in front of a policeman with Azerbaijan and Turkish flags at the Ataturk Stadium in Bursa, northern Turkey, on 14 October 2009 (Mustafa Ozer/AFP)
Off

Azerbaijan's ruling party directly accused Turkey of stoking "artificial tensions” on Tuesday between the two countries over a headscarf ban imposed in Azerbaijani primary and high schools this week.

The New Azerbaijan Party, led by President Ilham Aliyev, singled out Turkish chief presidential adviser Oktay Saral and other officials from Turkey's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who had opposed the ban in social media posts.

The party said Turkish media outlets close to the AKP government were publishing reports about Azerbaijan that were "contrary to the facts" and warned that relations between the two countries could suffer.

Saral said on Monday that denying students wearing headscarves access to education in Azerbaijan was unacceptable and called on Baku to reverse the practice.

His comments came after footage of Azerbaijani students crying and protesting outside schools went viral on Turkish social media, putting pressure on Ankara to criticise the decision.

New dress code regulations for schools in Azerbaijan were adopted for students on 21 September and for teachers on 6 October.

Baku arrested at least 37 people for protesting against the headscarf ban on Monday, accusing them of violating public order. The government also reportedly throttled the internet the same day, cutting access to social media platforms such as X, TikTok and Instagram. 

“I have my hijab on, but they are not letting me study.” Protests have erupted in Azerbaijan on Monday after some schools have prevented female teachers and students wearing the hijab from entering schools after an informal ban https://t.co/iEEwF0Qqlc

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) October 13, 2026

Ankara has refrained from officially commenting on the issue despite Aliyev's strongly worded rebuke of Turkey last week.

That rebuke followed Baku's assessment that social media commentary targeting Azerbaijan was part of a government-backed campaign.

Saral is known for expressing personal opinions on a range of subjects on social media. His intervention nevertheless prompted Azerbaijan's ruling party to issue a lengthy statement addressing several points of contention in bilateral relations.

Azerbaijan-Israel ties face backlash

Beyond the headscarf issue, many Turkish users on X have criticised Azerbaijan's close relationship with Israel.

Azerbaijan's decision not to leave the UN hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address last month triggered a wave of negative commentary about Baku.

Demonstrations in Azerbaijan against the headscarf ban in the schools on Monday as internet access has been partially restricted in the country https://t.co/BjwneCM22Y

— Ragıp Soylu (@ragipsoylu) October 12, 2026

The party said Azerbaijan's relationship with Israel was based on international law and mutual interests. It also reiterated its support for the Palestinian people, noting that Baku had provided financial and humanitarian assistance to Palestine.

"The operations of the Embassy of the State of Palestine in Azerbaijan are also sustained through financial support from the Azerbaijani state," the statement said.

It added that Aliyev had repeatedly backed a two-state solution, with East Jerusalem as the capital of the State of Palestine.

Responding to criticism of the headscarf ban, the party said no state in the Islamic world had the right to dictate its will to other Muslim peoples, interfere in their internal affairs or regard itself as superior.

In what was widely seen as a jab at Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the party added that any claim to serve the unity of the Muslim world must be substantiated through cooperation on an equal footing and mutual respect, "rather than hegemonic tendencies".

Addressing the ban directly, the party said Azerbaijan was constitutionally a secular state.

"We believe that using sensitive issues such as head coverings as instruments of political manipulation and division serves neither the unity of the Turkish people nor the solidarity of the Muslim world as a whole," the statement read.

"Using issues of this kind as a means of political pressure against Azerbaijan is particularly unacceptable. We call on the AKP government to refrain from this harmful policy."

Azerbaycan’da tesettürlü bir kız öğrenci, arkadaşlarının yanında gözyaşları içerisinde sınıftan çıkarıldı. Hem kız öğrenci hem de arkadaşları gözyaşlarını tutamadı. https://t.co/I1qtDTygP2

— Odak TV (@OdakTV1) October 12, 2026

Translation:  In Azerbaijan, a veiled female student was removed from the classroom in tears in front of her friends. Both the student and her friends could not hold back their tears.

One nation, two states

Turkey and Azerbaijan share close linguistic, ethnic and cultural ties.

Turkey was Azerbaijan's leading backer during the second Nagorno-Karabakh war in 2020, providing drones, arms and ammunition, as well as deploying F-16s and special forces to help Baku win the war.

The party's statement recalled the principle of "One nation, two states," coined by the late Azerbaijani president Heydar Aliyev, but stressed that it did not erase the distinction between the two sovereign countries.

"It refers precisely to one nation and two independent states," the statement said. "Under no circumstances does this principle provide grounds for one state to interfere in the internal affairs of the other or impose its own political and ideological approaches upon it."

Turkey moves to defuse Azerbaijan headscarf row after Aliyev's rebuke
Read More »

The party warned that further irresponsible statements by Turkish officials could damage bilateral ties.

A senior Turkish official told MEE last week, following Aliyev's remarks, that Ankara had no intention of interfering in Azerbaijan's domestic affairs and that no official statement suggested otherwise.

"We believe this is a misunderstanding," the official said at the time, adding that Ankara had conveyed this message at the highest levels to reassure Baku.

Multiple Turkish officials said Ankara would not respond to the indirect criticism and would instead seek to ease tensions.

The senior official described Azerbaijan as a "kin country," highlighting the strategic energy, transport and military investments the two states had jointly developed and implemented.

The official played down the spat as inconsequential and said further engagement would ease tensions, as it had in the past.
